idea: Roblox buys a dying American mall and rebuilds it floor by floor as the most-visited teen hangout in Roblox, designed and governed by kids, as a headline-making rebuttal to a world that stripped young people of real places to gather.

Launch Klarna 3AM, a checkout curfew that holds every purchase made between midnight and 5am until morning, while billboards across cities anonymously broadcast the most unhinged abandoned carts of the night, making Klarna the first payments brand to tell you to sleep on it.

Roblox hands a dying American town's abandoned mall to its youngest players, who design the replacement inside the game while the town council legally binds itself to build the winning vote, making the first public building in history drafted, zoned, and decided by children.

Launch SKILSMÄSSA, a flat-pack furniture line designed to be split cleanly in two with the same Allen key that once started the fights, turning IKEA's couple-testing assembly ritual into the first home collection that helps people separate fairly and start over.

Klarna launches "Regret Receipts," a pop-up bureau where shoppers can pay to publicly auction their worst impulse buys, with every sale funding someone else's debt payoff, turning the shame of overspending into a live, shareable, slightly absurd confession ritual that reframes smoothing payments as honest, human, and forgivable.
Build the most-played kid-made Roblox map at full scale as a real public playground in a city that has none, with its twelve-year-old creator listed as lead architect on the construction permit.

Slack declares a global Inbox Bankruptcy Day, wiping every unread badge on earth at midnight and inviting CEOs to publicly sign a pledge that anything sent before today never needed a reply, turning notification guilt into a holiday and Slack into the brand brave enough to say less.

IKEA launches Splitsville, a furniture line engineered to be cleanly halved when couples break up, complete with wordless instruction manuals for the separation, a tribute to the showroom aisles where relationships have been quietly tested and sometimes ended for decades.

UNESCO turns twelve endangered heritage sites into blank white silhouettes across every map, search result, and travel ad for one day, restoring each only when enough people claim it by posting a personal memory of being there.

UNESCO begins inscribing grandmothers as World Heritage Sites, giving families official plaques and an "In Danger" status that sets off a global race to record their dialects, recipes, and lullabies before the last living archive goes silent.

Slack launches "The Quiet Quarter," a campaign where it deliberately goes offline for one hour every Friday afternoon worldwide, replacing every channel with a single auto-reply, "Nothing urgent was ever said here," and paying real companies to ban meetings, turning the sound of work stopping into a cultural movement.

UNESCO quietly "delists" a beloved World Heritage Site for a day, wiping it from maps, search results, and streaming backdrops worldwide, then lets the public vote on which fragile place disappears next unless they act, turning the abstract fear of cultural loss into a visceral, global withdrawal symptom.

Roblox hands its homepage to a kid-built "Parent Takeover Day" where children design and run a real-world town hall, setting household rules, chores and bedtimes for adults, who must log in as beginner avatars and ask permission to speak, finally showing the world who truly knows how to build society.

Klarna launches Future You, a checkout feature where an AI-aged version of your own voice calls from ten years ahead to either bless the purchase or beg you to abandon the cart, making the most criticized impulse-buy button the first one that talks back.

UNESCO quietly "delists" a beloved World Heritage Site for one day, wiping it from maps, search results, and GPS, so the public experiences its absence and rushes to defend it, turning "Imagine It Gone" into the first heritage campaign where losing something finally makes people feel what we stand to lose.
Open the Embassy of Roblox in a real capital city, staffed by teenage developers as diplomats who grant adults visas only after they pass an entrance exam written entirely by kids.

Launch the Republic of Roblox, a digital nation whose constitution, laws, and borders are written and voted on by players under sixteen, then formally petition the United Nations for recognition while making adults apply for visas to enter.

Slack covers cities in a "someone is typing..." bubble that never resolves, then publicly exhibits a million anonymously donated, deleted drafts of messages workers almost sent, turning workplace restraint into a global confessional called Almost Sent.

Slack stages a public funeral for the recurring meeting, complete with eulogies and a casket of calendar invites, while a Fortune 500 partner deletes every standing meeting company-wide for one day and publishes the reclaimed hours as a national "time returned" ledger.

On Black Friday, Klarna locks its own checkout for 24 hours and covers the first installment on anything shoppers still want after sleeping on it, turning the most impulsive shopping day of the year into the world's first Cooling Off Day.

Slack launches "The Unsent Folder," a limited-run service where, for one week, it lets burned-out employees anonymously publish the messages they typed and deleted at work, then turns the most relatable ones into a public art installation and a national conversation about what we really wish we could say at work.

Launch IKEA Undo, a breakup service where separating couples bring shared furniture to stores to be professionally disassembled, split into two flat packs, and handed reverse-order instructions so the world's most famous relationship test also becomes the way love ends gracefully.

Slack installs a live Times Square ticker showing the real-time salary burned by pointless recurring meetings nationwide, then pays cash bounties to any team that publicly kills one and replaces it with a channel, turning cancelled meetings into the year's most shared corporate flex.

Launch the world's first divorce-ready furniture range, where every sofa, bed, and dining table unscrews into two equal halves, packaged with a wordless pictogram manual for splitting up amicably, making IKEA the first home brand honest enough to furnish how love actually ends.

Klarna launches a "Regret Exchange," a pop-up where people trade impulse purchases they already regret for the receipts of strangers' guilt-free buys, then publicly auction the unredeemed shame online, turning "buy now, pay later" into "confess now, laugh later" and making Klarna the brand that finally admits shopping is emotional.

Roblox holds a real-world "Parents Day" where, for twenty-four hours, adults are handed their kids' avatars and Robux budgets and must live inside the game under their children's rules, with the best-played parent crowned in a televised ceremony hosted entirely within a Roblox stadium.

UNESCO announces it is "delisting" a World Heritage Site: the future, by publishing a fully realized list of everything humanity will lose by 2050 if nothing changes, then letting people nominate which lost wonders to save, with each vote funding real restoration and rewriting the list in public.

Klarna commissions a famous artist to create one masterpiece, slices it into four pieces, and sells each piece to a stranger on Pay in 4, so the four owners must reunite every year to display the whole work or watch it stay broken.

Slack launches "Quiet Quitting Day," a day when the app auto-replies to every after-hours message with the sender's own unread messages from last week, publicly ranking companies by response guilt and turning the world's most dreaded notification into a global, shareable confession about how work never really ends.

Klarna buys a superyacht and splits it into a million tiny monthly payments, giving every co-owner one random minute of annual deck time, livestreamed, turning the ultimate billionaire status symbol into the world's most absurdly democratic, jointly owned flex.

IKEA opens a pop-up "Divorce Showroom" where couples who just split can legally and ceremonially divide a fully furnished living room, with every piece flat-packed on the spot, labeled "yours" and "mine," and a free Allen key each to finally build separate lives.

UNESCO quietly "delists" a beloved World Heritage Site from the map for one week, replacing it with a blank space and a hotline where locals and visitors narrate what it means to them, forcing the world to feel loss before it happens and turning preservation from a plaque into a panic.

Launch Last Words, a day when voice assistants worldwide stop speaking English and instead speak only an endangered language, voiced by its final living speakers, so millions of people must learn the one phrase that would otherwise die with them.

Slack launches "The Quiet Quitting Line," a real office-hours hotline where burned-out workers anonymously leave voicemails venting about work, then Slack transcribes them into a public wall of unsent messages and installs a mute button in Times Square that silences ads citywide for sixty seconds whenever the call volume peaks.

IKEA launches Unbuilding, a service that dismantles a divorcing couple's shared home, splits it into two flat-packs with wordless instruction manuals for starting over, and rebuilds each half in a new place.

IKEA launches Unbuilding, a breakup service where couples' shared IKEA furniture is professionally disassembled and divided into two flat-packed halves, each with a fresh manual for starting over alone, turning the brand's most famous relationship test into its most honest one.

On Black Friday, Klarna switches itself off for 24 hours and replaces checkout with a Sleep On It button that holds your cart, rewards you for waiting, and publishes a live public ticker of impulse regret avoided, turning the brand's biggest criticism into its boldest flex.

Buy a dying American mall, let Roblox players redesign it in-game, then physically build the most-voted creations with the teenage builders credited and paid as lead architects, so the generation with no third places finally gets one.

Launch "Regret Resale," where Klarna buys back your most embarrassing impulse purchases at face value, then auctions them as museum-grade artifacts of human weakness, with the original buyer's confession as the placard, turning shame about spending into the most shareable currency in culture.

IKEA opens "The Breakup Department," where couples splitting up can divide their shared home by having every item scanned, assigned and fairly separated, then rebuilt as two fully furnished fresh-start apartments, with the flat-pack instructions rewritten as a wordless, illustrated guide to starting over.

UNESCO launches Last Speakers, a phone line where every endangered language gets its own number you can call to hear its final living speaker, and when that speaker dies, the number rings into permanent silence, live-announced on global news as a cultural obituary.

For one day, UNESCO partners with voice assistants so billions of phones answer every request in a language with fewer than ten living speakers, recorded by those last voices, and titled "Last Words, No Backup."

Launch SPLIT, a sofa, bed, and bookshelf range engineered to separate into two equal halves with the included Allen key, turning IKEA's famously relationship-testing assembly into the world's first furniture built for amicable breakups, complete with a showroom "Divide and Part" checkout lane.

Launch Obby Court, where kids settle screen-time disputes by building a custom obstacle course their parents must beat to win the argument, with livestreamed trials, celebrity judges, and the most absurd verdicts turned into real, signed family contracts.

On Black Friday, Klarna blacks out checkout across every partner store for 24 hours, replacing it with a pink screen that holds your cart and asks "Still want it tomorrow?", turning the loudest impulse day of the year into the first public festival of delayed desire.

Launch Reverse Parental Controls, a Roblox tool where kids build real-world obbies with checkpoints, leaderboards, and rewards that parents must complete, from phone-free dinners to learning the emote, so adults finally have to play by the rules of the platform they dismiss.

Slack launches "Quiet Quitting Day," a real company-wide shutdown where it disables its own platform for 24 hours worldwide, replacing every workspace with a single auto-reply reading "Everyone's offline, including us," and pledges to donate the day's lost revenue to burnout research, turning its own absence into proof of its value.

Slack announces "Reply All Funerals," a real service where companies hold mock memorials for the dead meetings, pointless threads, and ghosted channels they're finally archiving, complete with eulogies read from actual message histories, then a public Slack-wide "Mute for Good" ceremony streamed live as workplace catharsis.

UNESCO places boredom, getting lost, and handwriting on a "Heritage in Danger" list, then designates phone-free pockets of real cities as temporary protected zones where visitors surrender their devices at the gate to experience what is vanishing.

UNESCO temporarily "delists" the ten most overphotographed World Heritage sites, blacking them out of every map and camera filter for one day, so the only way to see them is through the unfiltered stories of the locals who live beside them.

UNESCO launches Last Will of Humanity, letting anyone legally bequeath a grandmother's lullaby, dialect, or recipe to a public heritage registry, then publishes each inheritance as an endangered "species" that disappears from the world's archive unless strangers adopt and perform it.

Buy a dead American mall and hand its redesign to a rotating council of teenage Roblox creators, who must build every store, rule, and ridiculous feature in-game first, with only the most-played versions earning the right to become real concrete.

Slack launches "The Quiet Quarter," a company-wide offline day where it deliberately shuts down for every user at 3pm on a Friday, replacing all channels with a single auto-reply reading "Nothing here is as urgent as you think," then publishes the anonymized data on which messages people secretly missed least.

Klarna buys a Super Bowl spot and airs one quarter of a single film in each quarter of the game, the screen literally "paid in four," so the full ad only exists for viewers who stay to the end, while the internet obsessively pieces it together and argues about what's missing.

IKEA launches a Breakup Service where staff visit separating couples, dismantle their shared flat-pack home, and repack it into two boxes with new instructions for rebuilding it as two separate single-person homes, turning the brand's infamous couples' argument into a fresh start.
